We are arguably in the midst of the biggest technological revolution in US history.

tweets.text:
US productivity growth is accelerating:

US labor productivity rose +1.4% annualized rate in Q2 2026, more than double the +0.6% expected.

This follows an upwardly revised +0.8% increase in Q1, marking the 5th consecutive quarter of productivity gains.

At the same time, US manufacturing productivity jumped +1.9%, driven by a +4.6% surge in output, the strongest increase since Q4 2021.

However, these productivity gains came at the expense of workers, with inflation-adjusted compensation falling -3.2%, the largest quarterly decline since Q4 2022.

Meanwhile, unit labor costs, which measure how much a company pays workers to produce one unit of output, rose just +1.3% last quarter, well below the +2.1% expected.

The productivity boom is gaining momentum.

BREAKING: Global physical gold-backed ETFs posted +$3.0 billion in inflows in July, the largest monthly intake since April.

This pushed global gold ETF holdings up +23 tonnes, to 4,068 tonnes, just below the all-time high of 4,176 tonnes posted on February 27th.

European funds led, at +$2.1 billion, followed by Asia, at +$600 million, and North America, at +$71 million.

Year-to-date, global gold ETFs have attracted +$11.0 billion in inflows.

Global gold demand is rapidly recovering.

US refiners have shifted away from Saudi oil:

US imports of Saudi Arabian crude fell to zero in July, marking the first full month without imports since 1985, according to preliminary US government data.

This marks a sharp reversal from March, when US refiners were purchasing more than 800,000 barrels of Saudi crude oil per day.

This comes as US refiners sought alternative supplies after the closure of the Strait of Hormuz and broader Iran War-related disruptions pushed Middle Eastern crude prices higher.

As a result, Venezuela has emerged as the primary replacement, with US imports of its crude surging to ~600,000 barrels per day in July, up from just ~100,000 barrels per day at the start of the year.

Global oil trade flows are undergoing a historic shift.

The US economy lost jobs and the unemployment rate fell in the same month.

Payrolls dropped 23,000 in July against the 85,000 Wall Street expected, and May and June were revised down another 103,000. The unemployment rate slipped to 4.1% only because people quit looking, participation just hit its lowest since the 1970s.

Stocks and bonds both jumped and September rate-hike bets got cut. A labor market rolling over is what takes hikes off the table.

The falling unemployment rate is a mirage built on a shrinking workforce. Jobs are contracting, and the Fed just lost its reason to hike.

Copper is closing in on a new record and demand has almost nothing to do with it.

London copper blew past $14,000 a ton, near its $14,500 record, while the inventories backing the world's most-traded contract have drained more than 40% since May. The US and China are fighting over the same metal, and Trump's tariff threat has traders hoarding it on US shores.

This is a supply squeeze and a trade-war grab, not a demand boom. Every data center, power grid, and EV runs on copper, so a squeeze here is a tax on the entire electrification build.

Tariffs are a price shock, not inflation. A copper squeeze raises the cost of building the future, and that bill lands on everyone wiring it up. $FCX

AI is finally minting profits, and the winners are garbage haulers and HVAC makers, not the hyperscalers spending trillions to build it.

The average margin boost S&P 500 companies credit to AI jumped from 20 basis points last quarter to 150 this one. Waste Management's smart trucks alone now throw off more than $300 million a year.

The money is landing on the users of AI, not the builders financing it. That is why the equal-weight S&P 500 and small caps are outrunning the megacaps carrying all the debt.

The hyperscalers own the $2.6 trillion bill. The boring companies using their tools own the margin.

tweets.text:
A single tech trade made 225% in a year, then lost almost 40% in one month.

That is a long-short bet on US tech momentum, buying the winners and shorting the losers. The last spike up ran bigger than anything the dot-com bust or 2020 produced. Then a levered fund got caught on the wrong side and dumped into the reversal, making it worse.

When a crowded quant trade unwinds, the damage lands first on the most-owned names, the M7 and the AI complex everyone financed the same way.

Concentration like this gives no warning before it breaks. The next forced unwind hits the stocks in your index fund hardest.

tweets.text:
In 2000, the average stock stopped climbing months before the Nasdaq rolled over. Breadth cracked first, then the index followed.

Today the opposite holds. The equal-weight average stock is making new highs right alongside the S&P 500 and the Nasdaq, even after tech whipsawed last month. Broad participation like that is what a healthy bull looks like.

Money is still flowing into the whole market, not a handful of names. Tops do not form while the average stock is still rising.

Watch the average stock more than the headline index. The day it rolls over while the S&P 500 grinds higher on the M7 alone is the day to get defensive.

Oil is spiking on Iran again, and the same crowd is screaming tank bottoms and $200 crude.

The world has drawn down 400 to 600 million barrels since March, real and large. What the panic skips: China still sits on roughly 1.3 billion barrels of strategic reserve, and rich nations hold about another billion. Depleted, nowhere near empty.

A Hormuz spike is a supply shock, a one-time tax on growth, not inflation. Only the printing press makes inflation, and a tanker stuck off Iran does not run the press.

Betting on permanently higher oil, or an inflation scare out of crude, is betting the cushion is gone. It is not. The spike fades, the tax stings for a quarter, and money printing stays the only thing that makes real inflation.
